initial_requirements: The Gaia science-processing community needs a fast simulator that can generate catalog, auxiliary, intermediate, and statistically representative final-mission data for Gaia instruments. Users should be able to select the processing stage and relevant error models, produce large simulated datasets without running the full telemetry and mission-database chain, and deliver results compatible with the wider Gaia processing environment as scientific models evolve.

slots.key: Versioning requirements for evolving scientific models
slots.value: Configuration artefacts should be versioned clearly so it is obvious which scientific model or error model they belong to; the simulator should keep track of the exact configuration used for a run, including parameter files and the random seed; users should be able to select a saved configuration rather than rebuilding it manually; adjusted scenarios should record explicit differences so runs remain auditable and rerunnable/reproducible. Results should also be traceable back to the configuration that produced them, and the run should be reproducible later or adaptable cleanly for a new scenario. When reusing a saved configuration, the latest approved version that matches the intended processing stage and science use case should be selected; if multiple variants exist, the one tied to the same validation baseline or campaign context should take precedence over a newer but unvetted option. If the saved configuration differs from the current scenario in a way that affects output meaning, it should not be silently reused; it must be explicitly adapted or treated as a new configuration. Minor operational differences may be overridden if they do not change interpretation, but any scientific difference must be surfaced and checked. Updated scientific models should be treated as versioned inputs so outputs stay tied to a known model set; new behavior should be introduced only in a controlled release with traceability in the output to identify which model version generated it. If a newer model would break compatibility with existing downstream Gaia processing, the older path should be preserved or a switch provided until the wider environment catches up. Model evolution should be explicit and managed, not automatic or surprising. The produced result must also be traceable back to the exact input configuration and the simulator version that created it, with durable references to the full run settings, model versions used, and relevant environment or transformation identifiers; if that chain cannot be reconstructed, the output is not fully auditable for comparison or reproduction.

Fidelity-speed tradeoff by simulation stage
slots.value: Default to fast execution for routine testing and iteration; earlier stages like catalog or quick intermediate runs should stay within minutes to maybe under an hour for normal use, since they are rerun often while tuning inputs. Heavier final-mission style simulations may take a few hours if still meant for routine validation, but beyond that they become special-purpose batch jobs. If a run exceeds that, use a reduced-fidelity mode, a smaller sample, or a staged run that lets people check results incrementally instead of waiting for the full dataset. For stage selection, guide users by asking what they want the data to be used for rather than requiring internal pipeline terms: quick algorithm testing should steer to an earlier or lighter stage, while realistic end-to-end behavior should suggest a later or final-mission stage with relevant errors included. Defaults should be the most common safe choice for that use case, with a short explanation of the fidelity gained or lost by moving earlier or later in the chain. If stage choice materially affects interpretation, warn before running but still allow an experienced user to override.

slots.key: Automatic assembly of standard configuration pieces
slots.value: The simulator should automatically assemble standard, repeatable pieces such as selected stage defaults, the compatible error model set, and the usual metadata needed to make the output look like a Gaia product. Required entities are the ones that define the run unambiguously, like the selected processing stage, the source or population definition, and the specific error model or model set if that stage depends on one. Optional entities are extra metadata, comments, or convenience defaults that do not change the scientific meaning of the output. If a needed entity is missing, the simulator should fail fast and tell the user exactly what is missing; if it is ambiguous or incompatible with the chosen stage or error model, it should ask for disambiguation or reject the configuration with a clear reason rather than guessing silently. Harmless convenience defaults that do not affect scientific interpretation may be accepted with a warning, while anything nonstandard or scientifically consequential must be confirmed before the run can proceed. If the auto-filled choice would narrow the run to only certain downstream products, or if it depends on a processing variant that isn’t explicitly intended, the simulator should stop and ask for confirmation rather than assume the user wants that path. It should also ask for confirmation if the metadata would make the output look valid while actually steering it into a special-case interpretation, to avoid silent scientific mistakes.

slots.key: Runtime cap or lighter alternative for high-fidelity runs
slots.value: Earlier stages such as catalog or quick intermediate runs should stay within minutes to under an hour for normal use, since they will be rerun often while tuning inputs. Heavier final-mission style simulations can take a few hours if they are still meant for routine validation, but beyond that they become more like special-purpose batch jobs. If a run would exceed that, the fallback should be a reduced-fidelity mode, a smaller sample, or a staged run that allows incremental checking instead of waiting for the full dataset.

slots.key: Validation tolerance rules by run type
slots.value: Tolerances should not be a single universal bound; they should vary by output type and intended use of the run. Exploratory or representative simulations can use reasonable statistical tolerance, while regression checks or calibration-like comparisons should use much tighter bounds aligned with the relevant Gaia pipeline stage. If stage choice materially affects interpretation, the tool should warn the user before they run, but still allow an experienced user to override it. Anything that affects the astrophysical content, calibration assumptions, source classification, the exact error-model application, or which Gaia processing variant or downstream product the data is meant to support should always require a person to verify it before output is produced. Low-risk cases like formatting conveniences, file naming, ordering, or filling in clearly implied defaults where the scientific interpretation stays the same can proceed on their own, but any doubt about whether the meaning changes should be treated as needing verification.

slots.key: Near-zero or disabled tolerance cases
slots.value: Tolerance should be effectively disabled or near-zero for exact schema compatibility checks, deterministic transforms, and legacy reproduction. For bit-for-bit or row-for-row consistency runs, any deviation should be treated as a failure rather than accepted within a loose validation window. When tolerance is effectively zero, anything that is part of the release contract for that release must match exactly, or within a very narrowly defined, documented exception. Minor differences are only acceptable if they are purely non-scientific, such as ordering that doesn’t affect interpretation, metadata timestamps, or formatting that doesn’t change the content. Anything that could alter a downstream result or break reproducibility is a failure in this mode.

slots.key: Error model precedence and combination rules
slots.value: Precedence should be explicit in the run configuration rather than inferred from order or names. Overlapping models should only be combined when that combination is defined as valid; otherwise they should be treated as mutually exclusive and the configuration rejected or narrowed to one model. A pipeline-stage-specific model should override a generic default when both are present. If there is any risk of double-counting the same effect, one model should be suppressed and the decision logged rather than quietly applying both.

slots.key: Criteria for deferring optional simulator capabilities
slots.value: Leave a capability out of the current release if it is not needed to produce the core Gaia data products at the chosen processing stage, does not block realistic campaign scale or compatibility, or can be modeled acceptably with a simpler approximation for now. Capabilities that are operational multipliers with the least scientific value per unit cost should be capped or redesigned first, while science-defining inputs such as the source catalog should be protected. Repeated intermediate-product generation and extra error-model combinations are typical first candidates for capping before source catalog size. If output storage or export throughput is the bottleneck, it can become the first thing to cap or redesign because it blocks everything else.

slots.key: Conditions requiring earlier inclusion of optional simulator capabilities
slots.value: Include a capability sooner if people cannot validate results without it, if omitting it would make outputs incompatible with the wider processing environment, if it changes the scientific credibility of the simulator, or if it becomes necessary for the main user workflows. Model evolution should be explicit and managed, not automatic and surprising; updated scientific models should be introduced through controlled releases, outputs should retain traceability to the model version that generated them, and if a newer model would break downstream Gaia processing compatibility, the older path should be preserved or a switch provided until the wider environment catches up.
